text:
Ecological site R155XY050FL (155X): Loamy and Clayey Freshwater Floodplain Marshes and Swamps General information - Ecoclass name: Loamy and Clayey Freshwater Floodplain Marshes and Swamps
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very poorly drained loamy and clayey soils on floodplains in central and south Florida. These sites are frequently flooded for brief to very long durations and will usually correlate with seasonal rainfall patterns during the summer months. Soils will have an argillic horizon within 20 inches of the surface. The organic matter content of the surface layer is dominantly medium or high. The presence of these subsurface horizons at the given depths will attribute to specific production values in managed states compared to soils with similar horizons at different depths on similar landforms. Dominant vegetation within this site correlates with Florida Natural Area Inventory communities "Floodplain Marsh" and "Floodplain Swamp". These sites are adapted for harsh environmental conditions including flooding for extensive periods of time, resulting in highly anaerobic conditions. Extensive loss of natural habitat can be attributed to anthropogenic activities of installing water control structures to drain water for urban and agricultural uses.

Surface water runoff from agriculture and urbanization are carefully monitored to help mitigate sinkhole development. The major soil resource concerns are wind erosion, maintenance of the content of organic matter and productivity of the soils, and management of soil moisture. Conservation practices on cropland generally include conservation crop rotations, cover crops, irrigation water management (including micro irrigation systems), nutrient management, and pest management. Conservation practices on pasture and rangeland generally include prescribed grazing, brush management, pest management, prescribed burning, and watering facilities. Conservation practices on forestland generally include forest stand improvement, forest site preparation, prescribed burning, firebreaks, establishment of trees and shrubs, pest management, and management of upland wildlife habitat.

Water features - Water features: These wetlands are primarily influenced by over-bank flow from connected riverine systems. Rainfall and runoff from upland communities as well as groundwater flow into the riverine system will attribute to the naturally seasonal high water table. Water will move laterally as a massive, slow moving, overland sheet water flow following the low landscape, resulting in minimal deposits of alluvial materials. There is usually a delay between the onset of rainfall and the peak river flows that causes the wetland inundation. Seasonal patterns of water flow in floodplain wetlands occur primarily during the mid-summer months into the early winter months (July through December) and is attributed to rainfall during summer storms. This will be reflected by above ground surface water conditions during these months followed by a seasonal high-water table of 0 to 18 inches during the midto late-winter months into early summer (January through June). Events often associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, drought, or El Niño / La Niña climate patterns can shift the seasonal water inputs longer or shorter than the average wet seasons.

text: bird species. Insects such as mayflies (Ephemeroptera), larval flies (Diptera), midges (Chironomidae), and mosquitoes (Culicidae) use these habitats as spawning habitat. Many of these insects are prey to species such as dragonflies and damselflies (Odonata). Floodplain wetlands provide a biodiverse habitat for fish species, especially larger species. These habitats are more diverse than isolated depressional wetlands as the seasonal overflow of a riverine system in which the fish are permanent residents becomes more extensive. Some fish utilize these wetlands to complete their lifecycle, primarily for spawning and as nursery areas for juvenile fish which require slow moving water. These floodplain wetlands also create more available feeding grounds, which are usually rich in invertebrate prey because of the presence of decaying plant material, algae, and other food sources. Common fish in these wetlands include sunfish (Lepomis spp.), bass (Micropterus spp.), crappie (Pomoxis nigromaculatus), and minnows (Notropis spp.). Larger reptiles such as the American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis), common cooters (Pseudemys floridana), and common snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentine) utilize close proximity to the wetlands as feeding areas, while utilizing upland wetlands for nesting areas.

text: Larger reptiles such as the American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis), common cooters (Pseudemys floridana), and common snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentine) utilize close proximity to the wetlands as feeding areas, while utilizing upland wetlands for nesting areas. Aquatic vegetation found in these wetlands provides abundant supplies for birds and other wildlife with food, foraging ground, nest-building areas, nurseries, and shelter from both weather and predators. Many birds have become adapted to exploit these wetland habitats via increased leg length and bill shape. Other important adaptations include webbed feet, rear leg placement, and water-resistant feathers are utilized by resident and migratory bird species to be successful in these habitats. Seasonal variations in water level, temperature, and supply of prey species will influence changes in species composition in marshes. Common species include herons, egrets, bitterns, rails, ibis, limpkins (Aramus guarauna), wood storks (Mycteria americana), snail kites (Rostrhamus sociabilis), and Florida sandhill cranes (Grus canadensis pratensis). Different species will utilize these different habitats in different ways, but often serve as indicators of wetland ecosystem integrity due to their close association with a particular community.

Ecological site R155XY060FL (155X): Organic Freshwater Floodplain Marshes and Swamps General information - Ecoclass name: Organic Freshwater Floodplain Marshes and Swamps
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very poorly drained organic soils on floodplains in central and south Florida. These sites are frequently flooded for very long durations and will usually correlate with seasonal rainfall patterns during the summer months. Soils will have organic material directly over bedrock or organic material over sandy, loamy, or clayey marine or alluvial deposits with the lack of a diagnostic subsurface horizon. These organic soils will attribute to specific production values in managed states from legacy soil surveys compared to mineral soils with different diagnostic horizons at variable depths on similar landforms. Dominant vegetation within this site correlates with Florida Natural Area Inventory communities "Floodplain Marsh" and "Floodplain Swamp". These sites are adapted for harsh environmental conditions including flooding for extensive periods of time, resulting in highly anaerobic conditions. Extensive loss of natural habitat can be attributed to anthropogenic activities of installing water control structures to drain water for agricultural uses.

text:
Water features - Water features: These wetlands are primarily influenced by over-bank flow from connected riverine systems. Rainfall and runoff from upland communities as well as groundwater flow into the riverine system will attribute to the naturally seasonal high water table. Water will move laterally as a massive, slow moving, overland sheet water flow following the low landscape, allowing for the build up of organic matter. There is usually a delay between the onset of rainfall and the peak river flows that causes the wetland inundation. Seasonal patterns of water flow in floodplain wetlands occur primarily during the mid-summer months into the early winter months (July through December) and is attributed to rainfall during summer storms. This will be reflected by above ground surface water conditions during these months followed by a seasonal high-water table of 0 to 12 inches during the midto late-winter months into early summer (January through June). Events often associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, drought, or El Niño / La Niña climate patterns can shift the seasonal water inputs longer or shorter than the average wet seasons.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Water Table Dynamics Due to the flat topography of this MLRA, minimal gradients, high precipitation amounts, and seasonal temperature changes, there are often extreme fluctuations of the water table between summer and winter months. As water accumulates in the adjacent systems it needs to reach maximum water holding capacity before overflowing into the floodplain communities. Water will be temporarily held in these wetlands during the summer months and then slowly released into the groundwater aquifer (Florida Aquifer System) or recede via evaporation or evapotranspiration during the winter months (Haag et. al, 2010). Changes in wetland community distributions are dependent on local environmental conditions such as cyclical changes in precipitation and community disturbances such as fire suppression and anthropogenic alterations to surrounding habitats (ditching, drawdown of water table). Drier conditions may contribute to an increase in conversion of marsh wetlands to shrub-scrub or forested wetland communities. Plant Community Dynamics Changes in vegetation in these communities are often distributed via slight changes in hydroperiod that cannot be met with our current scale of mapping, resulting in two naturalized states of forested and non-forested wetland systems. Along the wetland edges, in the upland transition zone, more mesic species and ecological communities of poorly drained sites such as hydric savannas and hydric forests may occur.

Seasonal flooding is the main ecological driver for both forested and non-forested states. This extended hydroperiods is necessary to maintain the plant compositions and provide oxygen and nutrient inputs. The understories of these communities will vary seasonally, and will often be inundated to various depths in the summer months and support floating aquatic emergent and persistent emergent herbaceous species. In the winter months when water is receding or absent the understory will often support non-persistent emergent herbaceous and hydrophytic grasses. Seeding of cypress seeds and other hardwoods in dry years (where hydrology is not altered) in a floodplain marsh may allow the introduction and establishment of these trees, creating a closed canopy floodplain swamp (Titus, 1991; Wetzel et. al, 2001). Extended loss of hydroperiods within non-forested systems may allow for the encroachment of shrubby woody species in the understory. In forested systems, a loss of hydroperiod may also result in the increase of shrubby woody species as well as other hardwood trees such as bays, gums, elms, oaks, and maples, creating a mixed hardwood forest (Titus, 1990). Disturbances Next to seasonal flooding, fire regimes are the second most important ecological process which influence this site, especially in non-forested wetland communities. Fire regimes will be specific to each individual community and will often enter from pyrogenic upland habitats and extinguish themselves. Natural fires were principally caused by lightning but have since been replaced by prescribed burning due to the fragmentation of these habitats from roads and other anthropogenic features. Fire is used to prevent woody encroachment into freshwater marshes and to promote flowering phenology of certain species. Fire in swamp communities is less common due the highly shaded ground conditions. During years when swamps are dry, peat fires may burn the roots of cypress trees, killing the plants and seeds and converting these areas to scrub - shrub wetlands and areas favoring replacement by willows and subsequent hardwoods (Coladonato, 1992). If the root systems are not killed following fire, cypress and other hardwoods will often sprout from the stumps when top killed. Without fire over extensive periods of time, bays and other hardwoods may increase in density and cause more rapid peat accumulation.

General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very poorly drained sandy soils in isolated depressions, drainageways, and low broad flats throughout central and south Florida. These sites are frequently ponded for long to very long durations and will usually correlate with seasonal rainfall patterns during the summer months. Soils will range from 40 inches to greater than 80 inches of fine sand or sand. Diagnostic subsurface horizons may include a spodic horizon, an argillic horizon below 40 inches, or both. Some soils may lack a diagnostic subsurface horizon. The organic matter content of the surface layer is dominantly medium or high. The presence of these subsurface horizons at the given depths (or absence of horizons) will attribute to specific production values in managed states compared to soils with similar horizons at different depths on similar landforms.

General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas of swamp and marsh. Sinkholes affect land use and management.

Water features - Water features: These wetlands are primarily influenced by rainfall and runoff from upland communities. Water will accumulate and collect into these isolated depressions across the landscape and will be temporarily held in these wetlands. As water inputs decrease and stop, water will be slowly released into the groundwater aquifer or recede via evaporation or evapotranspiration (Haag et. al, 2010). Flooding conditions may occur if the standing water depth is greater than the local topography, occurring as a massive, slow moving, overland sheet water flow until stopped by a local microhigh. Seasonal patterns of water accumulation occur primarily during the summer months (June through November) and is attributed to rainfall during summer storms. This will be reflected by ponding and flooding conditions during these months followed by a seasonal high water table of 0 to 30 inches during the winter months (December through May). Events often associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, drought, or El Niño / La Niña climate patterns can shift the seasonal water inputs longer or shorter than the average wet seasons.

Typical soils will range from 40 inches to greater than 80 inches of fine sand or sand. A mucky surface texture modifier may often be seen. Diagnostic subsurface horizons may include a spodic horizon, an argillic horizon below 40 inches, or both. Some soils may lack a diagnostic horizon. At times, restrictive features (most commonly lithic or paralithic bedrock or an ortstein horizon) occurs at moderately deep to very deep depths and may have subsurface limestone fragments ranging from 0 to 14%. The pH of the soil profile ranges from extremely acidic to neutral.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Water Table Dynamics These sites have a dynamic water table with extreme fluctuations between the winter and summer months. Rooting depth will often not be restricted solely by soil materials in these sites due to the sandy extent and depth to illuvial materials, but rather by duration of seasonal high water table saturation and ponding influences. Non-hydrophytic species may develop stress during the summer months when the water table is at or above the surface. Non-persistent emergent species may develop stress when water is absent during the dry winter months. Due to the seasonal change of water inputs in these communities, soil conditions will often oscillate between anaerobic and aerobic conditions and may allow for a thin layer of decomposed organic material to accumulate on the surface. Changes in wetland community distributions are dependent on local environmental conditions such as cyclical changes in precipitation and community disturbances such as fire suppression and anthropogenic alterations to surrounding habitats (ditching, drawdown of water table). Drier conditions may contribute to an increase in conversion of marsh wetlands to shrub-scrub or forested wetland communities. Plant Community Dynamics

Plant Community Dynamics Changes in vegetation in these communities are often distributed via slight changes in hydroperiod and geomorphology that cannot be met with our current scale of mapping, resulting in two naturalized states of forested and non-forested wetland systems. Along the wetland edges, in the upland transition zone, more mesic species and ecological communities of poorly drained sites such as hydric savannas and hydric forests may occur. In non-forested and forested communities dominated by a concave slope shape, species composition will often be driven by slight changes in hydroperiods, creating concentric zones of vegetation. The deepest zones will hold standing water for the longest periods of time whereas the shallowest zones will hold standing water for lesser periods of time. Configuration of hydroperiod changes between these zones will often result of more herbaceous species towards the deeper zones and more graminoids and forbs towards the shallower zones.

Disturbances Next to seasonal ponding, fire regimes are the second most important ecological process which influence this site. Fire regimes will be specific to each individual community and will often enter from pyrogenic upland habitats and extinguish themselves. Natural fires were principally caused by lightning but have since been replaced by prescribed burning due to the fragmentation of these habitats from roads and other anthropogenic features. Fire is used to prevent woody encroachment into freshwater marshes and prairies and to promote flowering phenology of certain species. Fire in swamp communities is less common and estimated the interior may go without fire for decades or even centuries while the exterior edges are exposed to more frequent fire dependent on the surrounding communities fire regimes. Without fire, bays and other hardwoods may increase in density and cause more rapid peat accumulation. Anthropogenic Influences

Anthropogenic Influences Many wetlands in Florida have been altered for anthropogenic use in the past and are continuously used in these altered states shown in the state and transition model. However, wetlands are currently protected at the Federal, State, and County level in Florida. Many wetlands have been converted back to their reference communities through the Wetlands Reserve Program (WRP) with assistance from Florida NRCS. The following altered states shown in the state and transition model should be used as guidance when creating land management plans on converted wetlands to prevent further loss to soil resources. text: bird species. Insects such as mayflies (Ephemeroptera), larval flies (Diptera), midges (Chironomidae), and mosquitoes (Culicidae) use these habitats as spawning habitat. Many of these insects are prey to species such as dragonflies and damselflies (Odonata). Many isolated wetlands consist also of amphibians and reptiles. Smaller amphibians and reptiles such as frogs, salamanders, turtles, and some species of water snakes utilize wetlands that are absent of large predator species such as alligators and large fish that would prey on them. Frogs and salamanders utilize these areas during their egg and larval stages, before moving to more upland habitats during their adult lives. Common species found in these wetlands may include the black swamp snake (Seminatrix pygaea), eastern mud snakes (Farancia abacura), common cooters (Pseudemys floridana), and common snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentine). Alligators may create localized depressions by thrashing called “gator holes” which retain water during dry periods and are utilized as refuges.

Fish in isolated wetlands will undergo seasonal stress during the dry season when water begins to recede to the lowest point in the landscape, often a dug-out gator holes which hold water year-round. These fish are often less than 6 inches long and adapted to a range of conditions that include low pH and low dissolved oxygen levels. Species may include the eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), redfaced topminnow (Fundulus cingulatus), least killfish (Heterandria Formosa), and blue spotted sunfish (Enmeacanthus gloriosus). In the wet season when ponding conditions are seen and isolated wetlands are connected, these fish will often transverse between different wetlands. These fish are omnivorous and will feed on algae, plant material, aquatic insects, and other invertebrates. These abundant fish in isolated depressions often act as prey for numerous other animals such as mammals like the racoon (Procyon lotor) and reptiles such as the American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) and multiple bird species.

Aquatic vegetation found in these wetlands provides abundant supplies for birds and other wildlife with food, foraging ground, nest-building areas, nurseries, and shelter from both weather and predators. Many birds have become adapted to exploit these wetland habitats via increased leg length and bill shape. Other important adaptations include webbed feet, rear leg placement, and water-resistant feathers are utilized by resident and migratory bird species to be successful in these habitats. Seasonal variations in water level, temperature, and supply of prey species will influence changes in species composition in marshes. Common species include herons, egrets, bitterns, rails, ibis, limpkins (Aramus guarauna), wood storks (Mycteria americana), snail kites (Rostrhamus sociabilis), and Florida sandhill cranes (Grus canadensis pratensis). Different species will utilize these different habitats in different ways, but often serve as indicators of wetland ecosystem integrity due to their close association with a particular community.

text: Mammals are not as abundant in these wetland communities as other animal species but will utilize these wetlands where and when abundant forage is found or for cover. Common species may include the racoon, marsh rabbit (Sylvilagus palustris), white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginanus), and feral hogs (Sus scrofa). Hogs are considered invasive species and damage community structure of marshes and swamps by uprooting areas, allowing for the introduction of invasive or non-native species. Interpretations - Recreational uses: These areas have limited recreational uses. In larger wetland communities these areas may be used for ecotours, birdwatching, and fishing. However, most of these areas occur in small extent and are not selected specifically for recreational areas due to frequent ponding. These areas are often used to provide opportunities for education and scientific activities. Interpretations - Wood products: Cypress is the most important wood product found and harvested primarily from the Forested Wetland communities. While there are currently no regulations to prevent logging of cypress in Florida, environmental protection regulations help preserve this cypress dominated wetlands. The Wetland Protection Act passed by the Florida legislature in 1984 prevents any forestry activity that significantly changes the wetlands or impairs the flow of water in, around or through a wetland. Ecological site R155XY080FL (155X): Sandy over Loamy Freshwater Isolated Marshes and Swamps General information - Ecoclass name: Sandy over Loamy Freshwater Isolated Marshes and Swamps
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very poorly drained sandy over loamy soils in isolated depressions, drainageways, and low broad flats throughout central and south Florida. These sites are frequently ponded for long to very long durations and will usually correlate with seasonal rainfall patterns during the summer months. Soils will range from 20 inches to 40 inches of fine sand or sand over a loamy subsoil (argillic horizon). The organic matter content of the surface layer is dominantly low to high. The presence of these subsurface horizons at the given depths will attribute to specific production values in managed states compared to soils with similar horizons at different depths on similar landforms.

Dominant vegetation within this site correlates with Florida Natural Area Inventory communities "Wet Prairie", "Depression Marsh", "Basin Marsh", "Dome Swamp", and "Basin Swamp". These sites are adapted for harsh environmental conditions including recurrent fires and ponding for extensive periods of time. These sites are found throughout the state often as small, isolated wetlands within larger pyrogenic upland communities. Extensive loss of natural habitat can be attributed to physical (hog rooting, over grazing, off-road vehicles) or chemical (agricultural, industrial, and / or urban runoff) disturbances that can destroy native species and allow for the introduction of non-native species. Draw down of the natural water table, through intentional artificial drainage or unintentional water control structures for upland agricultural and urban land uses may also allow for non-native species and woody encroachment into these sites.

Water features - Water features: These wetlands are primarily influenced by rainfall and runoff from upland communities. Water will accumulate and collect into these isolated depressions across the landscape and will be temporarily held in these wetlands. As water inputs decrease and stop, water will be slowly released into the groundwater aquifer or recede via evaporation or evapotranspiration (Haag et. al, 2010). Flooding conditions may occur if the standing water depth is greater than the local topography, occurring as a massive, slow moving, overland sheet water flow until stopped by a local microhigh. Seasonal patterns of water accumulation occur primarily during the summer months (June through November) and is attributed to rainfall during summer storms. This will be reflected by ponding and flooding conditions during these months followed by a seasonal high water table of 0 to 18 inches during the winter months (December through May). Events often associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, drought, or El Niño / La Niña climate patterns can shift the seasonal water inputs longer or shorter than the average wet seasons.

Ecological site R155XY090FL (155X): Loamy and Clayey Freshwater Isolated Marshes and Swamps General information - Ecoclass name: Loamy and Clayey Freshwater Isolated Marshes and Swamps
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very poorly drained loamy and clayey soils in isolated depressions, drainageways, and low broad flats throughout central and south Florida. These sites are frequently ponded for very long durations and will usually correlate with seasonal rainfall patterns during the summer months. Soils will have an argillic horizon within 20 inches of the surface. The organic matter content of the surface layer is dominantly medium to high. The presence of these subsurface horizons at the given depths will attribute to specific production values in managed states compared to soils with similar horizons at different depths on similar landforms.

Dominant vegetation within this site correlates with Florida Natural Area Inventory communities "Wet Prairie", "Depression Marsh", "Basin Marsh", "Dome Swamp", and "Basin Swamp". These sites are adapted for harsh environmental conditions including recurrent fires and ponding for extensive periods of time. These sites are found throughout the state often as small, isolated wetlands within larger pyrogenic upland communities. Extensive loss of natural habitat can be attributed to physical (hog rooting, over grazing, off-road vehicles) or chemical (agricultural, industrial, and / or urban runoff) disturbances that can destroy native species and allow for the introduction of non-native species. Draw down of the natural water table, through intentional artificial drainage or unintentional water control structures for upland agricultural and urban land uses may also allow for non-native species and woody encroachment into these sites.

General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas of swamp and marsh. Sinkholes affect land use and management.

Water features - Water features: These wetlands are primarily influenced by rainfall and runoff from upland communities. Water will accumulate and collect into these isolated depressions across the landscape and will be temporarily held in these wetlands. As water inputs decrease and stop, water will be slowly released into the groundwater aquifer or recede via evaporation or evapotranspiration (Haag et. al, 2010). Flooding conditions may occur if the standing water depth is greater than the local topography, occurring as a massive, slow moving, overland sheet water flow until stopped by a local microhigh. Seasonal patterns of water accumulation occur primarily during the summer months (June through November) and is attributed to rainfall during summer storms. This will be reflected by ponding and flooding conditions during these months followed by a seasonal high water table of 0 to 12 inches during the winter months (December through May). Events often associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, drought, or El Niño / La Niña climate patterns can shift the seasonal water inputs longer or shorter than the average wet seasons.

Ecological site R155XY100FL (155X): Organic Freshwater Isolated Marshes and Swamps General information - Ecoclass name: Organic Freshwater Isolated Marshes and Swamps
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very poorly drained organic soils in isolated depressions and low broad flats throughout central and south Florida. These sites are frequently ponded for very long durations and will usually correlate with seasonal rainfall patterns during the summer months. Soils will have organic material directly over bedrock or organic material over sandy, loamy, or clayey marine deposits with the lack of a diagnostic subsurface horizon. These organic soils will attribute to specific production values in managed states from legacy soil surveys compared to mineral soils with different diagnostic horizons at variable depths on similar landforms.

text: of a diagnostic subsurface horizon. These organic soils will attribute to specific production values in managed states from legacy soil surveys compared to mineral soils with different diagnostic horizons at variable depths on similar landforms. Dominant vegetation within this site correlates with Florida Natural Area Inventory communities "Depression Marsh", "Basin Marsh", "Dome Swamp", and "Basin Swamp". These sites are adapted for harsh environmental conditions including recurrent fires and ponding for extensive periods of time. These sites are found throughout the state often as small, isolated wetlands within larger pyrogenic upland communities. Extensive loss of natural habitat can be attributed to physical (hog rooting, over grazing, off-road vehicles) or chemical (agricultural, industrial, and / or urban runoff) disturbances that can destroy native species and allow for the introduction of non-native species. Draw down of the natural water table, through intentional artificial drainage or unintentional water control structures for upland agricultural and urban land uses may also allow for non-native species and woody encroachment into these sites.

Water features - Water features: These wetlands are primarily influenced by rainfall and runoff from upland communities. Water will accumulate and collect into these isolated depressions across the landscape and will be temporarily held in these wetlands. As water inputs decrease and stop, water will be slowly released into the groundwater aquifer or recede via evaporation or evapotranspiration (Haag et. al, 2010). Flooding conditions may occur if the standing water depth is greater than the local topography, occurring as a massive, slow moving, overland sheet water flow until stopped by a local microhigh. Seasonal patterns of water accumulation occur primarily during the summer months (June through November) and is attributed to rainfall during summer storms. This will be reflected by ponding and flooding conditions during these months followed by a seasonal high water table of 0 to 36 inches during the winter months (December through May). Events often associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, drought, or El Niño / La Niña climate patterns can shift the seasonal water inputs longer or shorter than the average wet seasons.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Water Table Dynamics These sites have a dynamic water table with extreme fluctuations between the winter and summer months. Rooting depth will often not be restricted solely by soil materials in these sites, but rather by duration of seasonal high water table saturation and ponding influences. Non-hydrophytic species may develop stress during the summer months when the water table is at or above the surface. Non-persistent emergent species may develop stress when water is absent during the dry winter months. Changes in wetland community distributions are dependent on local environmental conditions such as cyclical changes in precipitation and community disturbances such as fire suppression and anthropogenic alterations to surrounding habitats (ditching, drawdown of water table). Drier conditions may contribute to an increase in conversion of marsh wetlands to shrub-scrub or forested wetland communities. Plant Community Dynamics Changes in vegetation in these communities are often distributed via slight changes in hydroperiod and geomorphology that cannot be met with our current scale of mapping, resulting in two naturalized states of forested and non-forested wetland systems. Along the wetland edges, in the upland transition zone, more mesic species and ecological communities of poorly drained sites such as hydric savannas and hydric forests may occur.

Along the wetland edges, in the upland transition zone, more mesic species and ecological communities of poorly drained sites such as hydric savannas and hydric forests may occur. In non-forested and forested communities dominated by a concave slope shape, species composition will often be driven by slight changes in hydroperiods, creating concentric zones of vegetation. The deepest zones will hold standing water for the longest periods of time whereas the shallowest zones will hold standing water for lesser periods of time. Configuration of hydroperiod changes between these zones will often result of more herbaceous species towards the deeper zones and more graminoids and forbs towards the shallower zones. Areas dominated by linear slope shapes will have similar localized hydroperiods and support a more uniform species composition than concave areas. This will often be seen in low broad flats and larger depressional communities. Sites within a matrix of concave and linear slope shape areas will support more mixed stands of vegetation consisting of herbaceous emergents and graminoid species.

Ecological site R155XY110FL (155X): Wet Sandy Cutthroat Seeps and Flatwoods General information - Ecoclass name: Wet Sandy Cutthroat Seeps and Flatwoods
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with seepage communities along the transitional boundary between the Lake Wales Ridge (MLRA 154 - South-Central Florida Ridge) and the South Florida Flatwoods MLRA. The reference state plant communities are associated with poorly drained sandy soils on seepage slopes. Seeps occur as moist or wet places where subsurface water will exit the ground via horizontal movement along slope breaks. Water percolates vertically through upland communities until hitting an aquitard (loamy or clayey layer) or to the point where the ground water reaches the surface of the slope and begins to diffusely flow at or near the surface downslope.

upland communities until hitting an aquitard (loamy or clayey layer) or to the point where the ground water reaches the surface of the slope and begins to diffusely flow at or near the surface downslope. Reference plant community 1.1 is primarily composed of a dense herbaceous layer of cutthroat grass (Panicum abscissum). This is an endemic species specific to Florida and is maintained by receiving frequent fire and moisture from seepage. Extensive loss of habitat can be attributed to agricultural and silvicultural activates, fire exclusion, grazing, drainage, and soil disturbances (NatureServe, 2023). In the absence of fire these areas are readily encroached upon by shrubs and trees, creating open savannas to closed canopy forest habitats.
General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas of swamp and marsh. Sinkholes affect land use and management.

Water features - Water features: This site is influenced by seasonal rainfall and seepage. As rainfall penetrates upland associated communities it will percolate through the soil until hitting an aquitard (loamy or clayey layer that retards water movement) or to the point where the groundwater reaches the surface of the slope and begins to diffusely flow horizontally at or near the surface downslope. Seepage occur as moist or wet places where subsurface water will exit the ground via horizontal movement along those slope breaks. Seasonal rainfall in these sites will also attribute to the saturated ground conditions. Areas will reflect a seasonal high-water table ranging from 6 to 18 inches and may hold standing water if endoand epi-saturation are exhausted.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Water Table Dynamics This site is maintained by ground-water moisture from seasonal rainfall and seepage. Shallow ground-water flows downslope or near the soil surface for several months during the growing season from upland sites along the Lake Wales Ridge and other Central Florida ridgelines (Haag et. al, 2010). These conditions support the densely vegetated endemic cutthroat grass (Panicum abscissum), a stiff, strongly rhizomatous, turf-forming grass, which results in a large amount of both aboveand below-ground biomass production. The dominance of this grass is due primarily to both its soil-moisture relationship along slope breaks of Central Florida's ridges and maintenance by fire. Fire Recurrent low intensity fires are used to maintain the structure and composition of these communities, preventing woody succession. Frequent fire in the growing season (mid-April to late July) trigger flowering of cutthroat grass, whereas fire in the dormant season usually fails to trigger flowering (Kuhn & Root; NatureServe, 2023). Due to intense fragmentation of Florida's natural communities, prescribed burning is now the dominant form of fire management for this habitat.

Many of these communities have been reduced because of intense fragmentation and long-term fire suppression, creating closed canopy seepage forests dominates by bay species. Anthropogenic Activities This site has been highly altered due to extensive landscape alteration throughout Central Florida over the past 70 years. The reference community has been highly altered for different land uses such as rangeland, improved pastures, agriculture fields, and silvicultural stands (SCS, 1989; Sonnier et. al, 2023). Changes in hydrologic flow and length of hydroperiod of these seepage communities can also result in the growth of woody vegetation and decrease in biodiversity. Management to counter changes in hydrology may include more frequent, randomly timed, early growing-season fires to maintain desired community structure. Continued fire-suppression and drainage effects of surrounding lands are the greatest threats to this community.

text: Interpretations - Animal community: This community provides suitable habitat for multiple species. A dense, grassy understory provides suitable bedding habitats in the dry season for species such as white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and other large mammals. The dense cover of cutthroat grass also provides suitable habitat for snakes and other small ground dwelling predators. Overstory trees may provide suitable perching and nesting habitats for predatory bird species as well as songbirds. Live pine trees provide suitable habitat for the endangered red-cockaded woodpecker (Leuconotopicus borealis) compared to the softened wood of dead trees, typically habited by other woodpecker species. Rooting from wild hogs (Sus scrofa) have devastating impacts within this community and should be managed for their removal. Interpretations - Hydrological functions: Shallow groundwater flows downslope at or near the soil surface for several months each year (June to October, correlating with the average rainy season, but subject to change on yearly basis). Ecological site R155XY170FL (155X): Sandy Coastal Grasslands and Forests General information - Ecoclass name: Sandy Coastal Grasslands and Forests
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very deep somewhat poorly to moderately well drained sandy soils that exist behind active dune systems along the Florida coastline. These are found in greatest extent on barrier islands and capes along both the Atlantic and gulf coasts. This site often develops behind active beach dunes relying on the protection from intense sand burial and salt spray. This protection allows for the establishment of grasslands behind the dune system that support both salt and freshwater species.

text: Reference plant community 1.1 is primarily composed of open grasslands often large in size, narrow in width, running parallel along coastal beaches. These graminoids are well adapted to salt spray and sand burial and are able to readily re-colonize following disturbances. Disturbances that break through the protective barrier that supports these sites such as over wash and burial will often reset these areas to open bare sand until the seedbank present meets the correct conditions for growth. Without natural disturbances, the reference conditions may become encroached by salt tolerant woody species, and may transition to a closed canopy forest over time. These areas are highly urbanized due to desirable location in coastal communities and highly susceptible to degradation via foot traffic. This site may be split into two separate ecological site descriptions with future projects addressing saline influence on soil-vegetation dynamics. General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas

text: The landscape consists of nearly level to gently sloping marine terraces that have large areas of wetlands and marshes. Streams and lakes are common. Low-lying wet areas are flat with some hummocks that rise 3 feet (1 meter) above the general level of the landscape. Coastal areas consist of low beach ridges and dunes that rise 6 to 10 feet (2 to 3 meters) above the lower inland areas. Elevation ranges from sea level to less than 196 feet (60 meters), increasing gradually from the coast to inland areas.

Surface water runoff from agriculture and urbanization are carefully monitored to help mitigate sinkhole development. The major soil resource concerns are wind erosion, maintenance of the content of organic matter and productivity of the soils, and management of soil moisture. Conservation practices on cropland generally include conservation crop rotations, cover crops, irrigation water management (including micro irrigation systems), nutrient management, and pest management. Conservation practices on pasture and rangeland generally include prescribed grazing, brush management, pest management, prescribed burning, and watering facilities. Conservation practices on forestland generally include forest stand improvement, forest site preparation, prescribed burning, firebreaks, establishment of trees and shrubs, pest management, and management of upland wildlife habitat.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Water Dynamics These areas are influenced by both freshwater and saltwater dynamics. Rainfall will replenish the shallow subsurface freshwater lens which sits above the denser salt water. In lower areas freshwater may accumulate for brief periods of time after heavy rainfall. Due to their proximity to the coastline, community structure is often influenced by sea spray or salt spray. This spray is often most intense closer to the shoreline with active dune systems protecting the grasslands (1.1) and forests (1.3) behind it. As these systems build outward with dune migration, they become less influenced by salt in both the soil pores and wind borne salts. Freshwater tolerant grasses and shrubs will begin to replace the dominant salt tolerant grasses in both density and cover further inland. In wooded areas the spray will often kill the upper buds of the plants, producing smooth, pruned canopies. Further away from the shore, the maritime forest canopy gradually assumes a more uneven surface like an inland hammock communities as individual tree height becomes more of an expression of species growth potential rather than a growth response to an inhibitory environmental factor. Disturbances These areas are often dependent on active beach dune systems as protection from storm surges and will often become briefly flooded if the dune system is destroyed. Intense storms which break through a dune system may allow storm surges to enter these communities, where prolonged standing water and sand deposition may kill these species. Over time, excess salt is diluted by precipitation and flushed from the system, allowing for new growth after the beach dune has been re-colonized, starting with pioneer saline tolerant species, followed by more freshwater tolerant species. Absence of disturbances from the system may allow for the encroachment and establishment of woody species, creating maritime thickets (1.2) and eventually closed canopy hardwood forests (1.3). Under natural conditions coastal forests are unevenly aged, with mature oak and palm species present. Reproduction primarily occurs through canopy gaps. Fire is naturally rare and localized in this community with water barriers and sparse fuels combining to limit its spread. Anthropogenic Activities

on Rises, Ridges, and Knolls of Mesic Uplands General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with moderately well drained sandy soils found on ridges, rises, and knolls of interior and coastal Florida. Reference plant community 1.1 is primarily composed of a pine-oak scrub woodland with an open overstory of sand pine (Pinus clausa) and a dense understory of shrubby oaks and palmetto. These are fire maintained communities that rely on patchy burns to leave habitat for endemic species such as the Florida scrub jay. Fire frequency is dependent on the dominant species and available fuel load, and in the absence of fire these areas are readily encroached upon by shrubby oaks, creating a closed canopy forest. Due to the natural good drainage of these sites, extensive habitat loss is seen to agricultural and urban activities.
General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas of swamp and marsh. Sinkholes affect land use and management.

Conservation practices on pasture and rangeland generally include prescribed grazing, brush management, pest management, prescribed burning, and watering facilities. text: Soil features - Soil features: Soils are dominantly very deep, moderately to well drained sandy soils found in high elevations of sandy marine deposits. They will have 40 inches to greater than 80 inches of fine sand or sand. An argillic horizon may be present below 40 inches or is absent. Depth to bedrock is typically greater than 80 inches, but some locations may have root restrictions (ortstein, paralithic bedrock) at 20 inches to 80 inches. These have a wide range of taxonomic classification and will include: Typic Quartzipsamments (Archbold, Tavares), Spodic Quartzipsamments (Orsino, Dade, Welaka), Aquic Quartzipsamments (Satellite), Oxyaquic Alorthods (Pendarvis), Glossarenic Alorthods (Duette, Jonathan, Hobe), and Arenic Alorthods (Daytona). text: These are fire-maintained communities, relying on stand replacing intense fires to drive species reproduction and community maintenance. The reference community 1.1 consists of open shrublands, with or without an open canopy of pines, on dry, infertile, sandy habitats. Natural fire intervals for these communities are thought to be between 5 and 20 years, with upper and lower limits of fire return intervals being inferred from the life history traits of the dominant plants and / or the requirements of endemic animal species dependent on these communities (FNAI, 2010). These communities will often have a dense shrub layer that is variable among individual communities but will often consist of characteristic species such as shrubby oaks (Quercus myrtifolia, Q. geminata, and Q. chapmanii), Florida rosemary (Ceratiola ericoides), Fetterbush (Lyonia lucida), rusty staggerbush (L. ferruginea), saw palmetto (Serenoa repens), and scrub palmetto (Sabal etonia). These species will form a dense cover interspersed with patchy openings consisting of bare sand with a sparse cover of herbs and lichens, creating difficult ignition conditions. This often creates patchy unburned areas that are needed by endemic animal species such as the Florida scrub jay and sand skink for habitat until post fire recovery (FWC interpersonal communication). text: Plant Adaptations Rapid post-fire recovery (1- to 5-years) can be attributed to individual species adaptational responses to fire (e.g. resprouting, clonal growth, seedling recruitment) and individual community composition (Menges & Hawkes, 1998). The dominant overstory species sand pine (Pinus clausa) are fire dependent species, with serotinous cones that rely on intense heat to open for regrowth, typically dying off after fire due to thin bark (Carey, 1992). These trees begin to produce cones around 5 years and around 50 years begin to become more susceptible to root rot. If fire is too frequent these trees may not be old enough to reproduce, if fire is not frequent enough they may be replaced by oak. Florida rosemary also depends on fire-stimulated germination since it does not reproduce vegetatively, fire intervals of less than 10 years would deplete the seedbank and intervals greater than 40 years would allow species encroachment (Coladonato, 1992). Other shrubs such as saw palmetto, fetterbush, oaks, and rusty staggerbush are able to resprout from persistent root crowns and rhizomes after defoliated and top-killing the species. Absence of Fire / Succession In the absence of fire, understory shrubs (dominantly oaks) are no longer restricted from growing and may attain canopy heights, creating a closed canopy forest. With the establishment of a closed canopy forest, increased shading conditions and leaf litter create more mesic ground conditions, excluding the spread of fire throughout these systems. If fires do enter the system, the oak species are capable of re-sprouting quickly following injury due to large rhizome systems. Low intensity burns may be sufficient in reducing and maintaining groundcover integrity but are often insufficient in killing oaks. Intense burns during dry conditions may kill the overstory and revert the area back to an early successional shrubland. Many of these communities have been reduced because of intense fragmentation and long-term fire suppression, leaving behind small pockets of oak dominated forests. Altered Management

Altered Management While prescribed burning is the preferred method of scrub management, mechanical treatments such as roller chopping or mowing are short-term alternatives which may provide alternatives in areas where prescribed burning is infeasible (i.e. fragmented habitats surrounding urban cores). Stand management, through prescribed burning, mechanical treatment, or any other effort should leave patches to provide cover and foraging sites for species reliant on these communities while the scrub regenerates. Within the scrub vegetative community, there are different community variants based off fire history and slight speciation. Scrub habitats should be assessed on an individual basis and should be managed based on individual management plans. Many of these areas have been urbanized and are used for residential areas or agriculture, resulting in high fragmentation and loss of habitat. Many hiking and off-road trails are doubled as fire breaks due to the sensitivity of the natural community, and improper management of these trails can lead to increased soil erosion, especially along sloping portions of these communities. Scrub is also important for gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) and its associated commensals. Deep sandy soils with the absence of a restrictive layer and threats of a seasonal high-water table allow for gopher tortoises to create deep spreading burrows which may act as refuges for many species during disturbance events such as fires and hurricanes. The open overstory of scrub habitats also provide adequate sunlight for tortoise nests and thermoregulation, as well as providing an abundant food source in grasses and herbaceous species. In the absence of fire and growth of a closed canopy forest, tortoise populations may decline.

Many of the oak-dominated scrub communities are burned on intervals which correlate with the habitat requirement for the Florida scrub-jay. Oak height is a critical limiting factor for Florida scrub-jays which have been documented to abandon territories where the oaks reached >3 m and to suffer a net population loss in territories on Merritt Island on the Atlantic coast where patches of oak scrub in their territories were either taller than 1.7 meters or shorter than 1.2 meters. The lower limit of 5 years is based on the time required for re-sprouting oak stems to reach acorn-bearing height, acorns being an important part of the scrub-jay’s diet (FNAI, 2010). Ecological site R155XY220FL (155X): Sandy Coastal Beach Dunes General information - Ecoclass name: Sandy Coastal Beach Dunes
General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with very deep, excessively drained soils formed in sandy aeolian deposits. These are dune systems that form immediately adjacent to the Atlantic Ocean and gulf where there is sufficient wave and wind energy to deposit sandy materials. These are dynamic systems that actively move across the landscape, unless stabilized by vegetation. As these communities begin to stabilize and built in height and width, they begin to protect adjacent coastal communities found behind the dune system from intensive salt spray and tidal influences.

As these communities begin to stabilize and built in height and width, they begin to protect adjacent coastal communities found behind the dune system from intensive salt spray and tidal influences. Reference plant community 1.1 is primarily composed of salt-tolerant grasses and forbs that are able to rapidly colonize and outgrow sand deposition. Periodic disturbance events such as hurricanes may destroy the reference community and revert it to areas of open sand susceptible to wind movement until recolonization of vegetation. In the absence of disturbances these dunes may support more woody species along the backdune, stabilizing the dune. These areas are highly susceptible to erosion and are often traversed over by recreationalists to get to the ocean or developed for beachfront property. Intense urbanization of these areas may leave remaining habitats at risk for degradation or total loss of the community.
General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas of swamp and marsh. Sinkholes affect land use and management.

text: Climatic features - Climatic features: The climate of central and south Florida is warm to hot and temperate to subtropical, with this site getting an average annual precipitation of 51 to 59 inches (1295.4 to 1498.6 millimeters). Most rainfall occurs during moderate tropical storms that produce large amounts of rain from late spring through early autumn. Late autumn and winter are relatively dry. The average annual temperature is 69 to 76 degrees F (21 to 24 degrees C).

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Water Table Dynamics These areas are influenced by both freshwater and saltwater dynamics. Rainfall will replenish the shallow subsurface freshwater lens which sits above the denser salt water. These specialized dune plants root systems will often not be able to reach the freshwater lens during the dry season and often be subject to periodic drought conditions. Increased urbanization may lead to excessive withdrawals from the freshwater lens and coastal aquifers, lowering the water table and intensifying localized drought conditions. Salt Water Influence Sea spray or salt spray caused by breaking waves is generally greatest near the surf, often attributing to saline tolerant species colonizing these habitats. Periods of drought and intense constant spray as well as the poor moisture retention of sand makes these areas highly stressful for vegetative growth and typically dominated by a few hardy dune grasses and forbs. The zonation of intense, moderate, and minor salt spray is often dependent on local environmental conditions and distance from the shoreline.

text: These are highly fluctuating sediments deposited by wave and wind action from offshore bars, the tidal beach, the back beach above the high tide mark, and in existing dune systems. These active dune systems can rise higher than the surrounding habitat, being constantly built by sediment trapped and stabilized by growing vegetation (Davis, 1975). The vegetation which grows closest to the water is typically found at the base of the foredune system and are often the first species to colonize a beach community. These will help reduce the wind velocity and trap the sand, keeping it stable long enough for grasses to begin growing and forming a dune system. The reference community 1.1 is dominated by seaoats (Uniola paniculata) and other dune building perennial rhizomatous grasses, whose stems trap the sand grains blown off the beach, building up the dune by growing upward to keep pace with sand burial. These species are highly tolerant to the salt spray caused by breaking waves, and often expand by both seeds and lateral spread of rhizomes for the highest chance of survival. As vegetation increases on the dune system, these species will shade the soil, decreasing soil temperature and retaining more water from evaporation loss, allowing for the stabilization and succession of the backdune system. text: Disturbances These systems are highly susceptible to wind and wave erosion. Hurricane force winds can scour beach sand from the dune making it more susceptible to wave actions (Sallenger et. al, 2006). Extensive breaches may be widened and deepened by these severe storms and can often break through the dune system. These breakthroughs can destroy part of the dune system and may briefly flood the remaining dune system and habitats behind the dune dependent on its protection for their formation. Dune breakthroughs will often deposit outwash layers of sands and shells which may be rapidly colonized after water recession (Miller et. al, 2010). Water will recede after the storm back through the breakthrough, by evaporation, or through percolation. The intense input of salt water will stress and possibly kill the dune species, further making the dune more susceptible to erosion. Fire is naturally rare in this community due to constant sea spray as well as lacking the necessary fuel load to carry fire. Anthropogenic Activities / Resource Concerns

text: The major resource concerns for this ecological site are damage to the dune systems and its vegetation. The vegetative cover stabilizes the dune, preventing the movement of mobile sand. These areas are highly impacted by anthropogenic uses such as off-road vehicles and pedestrian foot traffic. Devegetated paths perpendicularly over the dune can funnel the wind and transport sand which may produce large dune blowouts. Degraded dune systems are more susceptible to erosion during storm events which can destroy interior coastal environments, subjecting them to excessive salt water flooding and sand burial. When dune systems become damaged restoration efforts may include human altered structures such as seawalls, ripraps, and dikes to prevent coastal erosion and deposition. Rebuilding the dune system artificially can include deposition of sand to extent the beach further out but is often an expensive process (Williams, 2007). Natural restoration of dune systems is often used when artificial building of dunes or structures is unfeasible and include replanting of native species (Miller et. al, 2010). Sand fences assist in more rapid sand deposition and dune grass planting generally speeds the natural revegetation process. Dune systems should be managed to avoid degradation via parallel paths over the dunes or boardwalks which reduce foot traffic. text: Latitudinal / Longitudinal Changes There may be a slight change in vegetative composition and structure along the two coastlines as well as slight shifts from temperate to subtropical species found in the north to south gradient. text: Interpretations - Animal community: These beach and dune systems provide critical habitat for both terrestrial and aquatic species. Many of these populations are rare, threatened, and/ or endangered due to increased urbanization. Aquatic species such as loggerhead sea turtles (Caretta caretta), green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas), and leatherback sea turtles (Derrmochelys coriacea) will utilize beach habitats during the nesting season (April through September). Mammals such as the southeastern beach mouse (Peromyscus polionotus niveicentris) utilize dune systems for habitat. These habitats also are very important for local and migratory bird species such as snowy plovers (Charadrius melodus), piping plovers (C. tenuirostris), and Wilson’s plover (C. wilsonia), which utilize the open sand and dune systems for nesting and breeding habitat as well as utilizing washed onshore wrack for forage. Other rare shorebirds include the American oystercatcher (Haematopus palliates), black skimmer (Rynchops niger), least tern (Sterna antillarum), and roseate tern (S. dougallii). on Ridges, Knolls, and Dunes of Xeric Uplands General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is associated with excessively drained sandy soils found on ridges, knolls, hills, and dunes of interior and coastal Florida. Reference plant community 1.1 is primarily composed of a pine-oak scrub woodland with an open overstory of sand pine (Pinus clausa) and a dense understory of shrubby oaks and palmetto. These are fire maintained communities that rely on patchy burns to leave habitat for endemic wildlife species such as the Florida scrub jay. Fire frequency is dependent on the dominant species and available fuel load, and in the absence of fire these areas are readily encroached upon by shrubby oaks, creating a closed canopy forest. Due to the natural good drainage of these sites, extensive habitat loss is seen to agricultural and urban activities.
General information - Mlra notes: This MLRA makes up about 19,973 square miles (51,731 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It stretches across the mid-section of the State, from the Gulf of America to the Atlantic Ocean, and north and south from the Everglades (MLRA 156A) to Jacksonville. This MLRA consists of a young sandy marine plain of Pleistocene age that is underlain by Tertiary-age limestone bedrock. The terrain is nearly level to gently sloping with large areas of swamp and marsh. Sinkholes affect land use and management.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Natural Fire These are fire-maintained communities, relying on stand replacing intense fires to drive species reproduction and community maintenance. The reference community 1.1 consists of open shrublands, with or without an open canopy of pines, on dry, infertile, sandy habitats. Natural fire intervals for these communities are thought to be between 5 and 20 years, with upper and lower limits of fire return intervals being inferred from the life history traits of the dominant plants and / or the requirements of endemic animal species dependent on these communities (FNAI, 2010). These communities will often have a dense shrub layer that is variable among individual communities but will often consist of characteristic species such as shrubby oaks (Quercus myrtifolia, Q. geminata, Q. inopina, and Q. chapmanii), Florida rosemary (Ceratiola ericoides), saw palmetto (Serenoa repens), and scrub palmetto (Sabal etonia). These species will form a dense cover interspersed with patchy openings consisting of bare sand with a sparse cover of herbs and lichens, creating difficult ignition conditions. This often creates patchy unburned areas that are needed by endemic wildlife species such as the Florida scrub jay and sand skink for habitat until post fire recovery (FWC interpersonal communication). Burned areas may revert the reference community 1.1 back to an early successional shrubland, reflecting similar species composition with changes in community structure.

Burned areas may revert the reference community 1.1 back to an early successional shrubland, reflecting similar species composition with changes in community structure. Plant Adaptations Rapid post-fire recovery (1- to 5-years) can be attributed to individual species adaptational responses to fire (e.g. resprouting, clonal growth, seedling recruitment) and individual community composition (Menges & Hawkes, 1998). The dominant overstory species sand pine (Pinus clausa) are fire dependent species, with serotinous cones that rely on intense heat to open for regrowth, typically dying off after fire due to thin bark (Carey, 1992). These trees begin to produce cones around 5 years and around 50 years begin to become more susceptible to root rot. If fire is too frequent these trees may not be old enough to reproduce, if fire is not frequent enough they may be replaced by oak. Florida rosemary also depends on fire-stimulated germination since it does not reproduce vegetatively, with fire intervals of less than 10 years would deplete the seedbank and intervals greater than 40 years would allow species encroachment (Coladonato, 1992). Other shrubs such as saw palmetto, fetterbush, oaks, and rusty staggerbush are able to resprout from persistent root crowns and rhizomes after defoliated and top-killing the species. text: Many of the oak-dominated scrub communities are burned on intervals which correlate with the habitat requirement for the Florida scrub-jay. Oak height is a critical limiting factor for Florida scrub-jays which have been documented to abandon territories where the oaks reached >3 m and to suffer a net population loss in territories on Merritt Island on the Atlantic coast where patches of oak scrub in their territories were either taller than 1.7 meters or shorter than 1.2 meters. The lower limit of 5 years is based on the time required for re-sprouting oak stems to reach acorn-bearing height, acorns being an important part of the scrub-jay’s diet (FNAI, 2010). It is estimated once the oaks grow into the overstory, they become a more suitable habitat for predator species such as Cooper’s hawk (Accipiter cooperii), sharp-shinned hawk (A. striatus), norther harrier (Circus cyaneus), merlin (Falco columbarius), and peregrine falcons (F. peregrinus). Other predators to Florida scrub-jays may include house cats, bobcats (Felis rufus), Eastern coach whips, eastern indigo snakes, and great horned owls (Bubo virginanus). text: General information - Ecoclass name: Subtropical Pine Flatwoods and Palmetto Prairie of Big Cypress General information - Ecoclass concept: The Subtropical Pine Flatwoods and Palmetto Prairie of Big Cypress ecological community are characterized by low flat lands with poorly drained sandy soils and an open overstory of pines with a dense grassy and / or shrubby understory. Frequent periodic disturbances are the biggest stressors of these communities. These areas are most common in the northwestern section of the Big Cypress ecoregion within this MLRA but may be found in higher landscape positions throughout the area. General information - Mlra notes: This area makes up about 7,749 square miles (20,071 square kilometers) and is entirely in Florida. It is located at the southern tip of the State and has shoreline on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of America. Lake Okeechobee borders the MLRA to the north. Aside from sugar cane plantations in the north, the Everglades National Park, Big Cypress National Preserve, and the Big Cypress Seminole Indian Reservation comprise this area. Historical ditching, berming, and canals prevent natural water flow through this delicate ecosystem. To mitigate this, extensive restoration efforts have been implemented. text: About one-third of this area is in Native American reservations, national parks, game refuges, or other large holdings. Cypress forests are extensive in the area, but mangrove forests are widespread along the eastern and southern coasts. A large part of the area is open marsh. Much of the area is used for hunting, fishing, and other recreational activities. The cropland in the area is used mainly for winter vegetables, but citrus fruits, avocado, and papaya are grown on the better drained soils. Sugarcane is an important crop on the organic soils south of Lake Okeechobee. The acreage of improved pasture is increasing. Beef cattle are the principal kind of livestock, but dairying is an important enterprise locally. Urbanization is extensive along the eastern coast.

The major soil resource concerns are wind erosion, maintenance of the content of organic matter and productivity of the soils, and management of soil moisture and soil subsidence. Conservation practices on cropland generally include conservation crop rotations, cover crops, nutrient management, pest management, water-control structures, surface drainage systems (field ditches, mains, and laterals), pumping plants, and irrigation water management (including micro irrigation systems and surface and subsurface irrigation systems). Conservation practices on pasture and rangeland generally include prescribed grazing, brush management, pest management, prescribed burning, and watering facilities. Conservation practices on forestland generally include forest stand improvement, firebreaks, pest management, prescribed burning, and management of upland and wetland wildlife habitat.

text: Physiographic features - Physiographic features: These areas are dominated by linear flatwoods that form in marine deposits. Slight changes in microtopography will often dictate species composition and hydroperiod. Micro-lows, or areas with slope shapes of linear – concave will reflect a seasonal high-water table of 0 to 6 inches and may hold standing water very long if endoand epi-saturation are exhausted after periods of heavy rain. Micro-highs, or areas with slope shapes of convex – linear will reflect a seasonal high-water table of 6 to 18 inches and may hold standing water briefly if endoand epi-saturation are exhausted after periods of extreme rain. Species composition may vary slightly based off the microtopography but will often reflect similar community structure and maintenance. These communities are often intermixed with one another and form a matrix of linear-concave, linear-linear, and convex-linear topography mapped within one soil component.

text: Geology: With its low-laying landmass, this area has been repeatedly submerged and exposed with variations in sea level over the past 50,000 years, creating thousands of feet of roughly horizontal geological layers rich in carbonates. The whole of Big Cypress ecoregion falls over the Pliocene series Tamiami Formation, a poorly defined lithostratigraphic unit containing a wide range of mixed carbonate-siliciclastic lithologies and associated faunas occurring at or near the surface. Fossils present in the Tamiami occur as molds, casts and original material. The fossils present include barnacles, mollusks, corals, echinoids, foraminifers and calcareous nannoplankton. The Tamiami Formation has highly permeable to impermeable lithologies that form a complex aquifer. Locally, it is part of the surficial aquifer system. In other areas, it forms a part of the intermediate confining unit/aquifer system (Scott, 2001). text: Climatic features - Climatic features: The climate of MLRA 156A is subtropical, with mild winters and hot wet summers. The average annual precipitation of this MLRA is 37 to 62 inches (950 to 1,565 millimeters). About 60 percent of the precipitation occurs from June through September. Most of the rainfall occurs during moderate intensity, tropical storms that produce large amounts of rain from late spring through early autumn. Late autumn and winter are relatively dry. The average annual temperature of the MLRA is 74 to 78 degrees F (23 to 26 degrees C). The freeze-free period of the MLRA averages 355 days and ranges from 345 to 365 days.

text: Water features - Water features: The flat topography creates minimal gradients, resulting in sufficient time for percolation, soil saturation and slow runoff that occasionally creates very poorly defined first-order ephemeral streams and typically results in sheet flow patterns if water becomes high. Where a soil hardpan is present, water moves slowly vertically relative to horizontal movement, through horizons above and below the hardpan layer. With standing water, wet flatwood soils may become waterlogged and poorly aerated during the rainy season. Mesic pine flatwoods soils can also become waterlogged and poorly aerated during the extreme rain events. This results in the saturated soils typical of unaltered, undrained mesic flatwoods. During the dry season, high evapotranspiration draws most of the water out of the upper soil horizons, drying them out. Soil moisture becomes depleted in the upper soil layers, above the hardpan, and a persistent drought condition frequently prevails through the dry season. As a result, during the dry season, groundwater is inaccessible for plants that cannot penetrate the hardpan. The most frequent and widespread hydrologic alterations typically result in reduced depth and duration of inundation, which tends to shift affected wetland plant communities towards shallower wetland types, or with sufficient drainage to upland types.

text:
The most frequent and widespread hydrologic alterations typically result in reduced depth and duration of inundation, which tends to shift affected wetland plant communities towards shallower wetland types, or with sufficient drainage to upland types. Water depths in flatwoods vary throughout the seasonal hydrologic cycle. With the onset of the rainy season, flatwoods may become quickly saturated. As the rate of precipitation exceeds the rate of runoff and percolation, standing water may begin to appear in the microlows in June. By July, flatwoods are uniformly wet. Deepest water levels are attained by the late rainy season in September. As the dry season begins in November the pattern reverses, with a shift to runoff and percolation exceeding precipitation. This results in the formation of isolated pools, as sheet flow recedes below the ground surface. The recession of the surface water is quick to reside after periods of rain as water drains to lower landscape positions.
Water features - Wetland description: Surface water ponding and soil saturation levels may vary from year to year based on local environmental conditions. According to the USDA-NRCS in Florida and the National Wetland Inventory (NWI), mesic and wet flatwoods are not considered wetland habitats but may have the potential to support wetland habitats. Location specific investigations are required to determine site specific conditions for wetland delineation.
